A fundamental driving force behind many of these initiatives will be the Recovery, Transformation and Resilience Plan (RTRP), presented by the Spanish Government inOctober 2020, which proposes assigning 39% of the funds that Spain receives under the Next Generation EU (NGEU) programme to the green transition; see Cansino et al. (2016) for a description of the policy measures to control carbon emissions in Spain. Ensuring that energy policies are as effective as possible requires an understanding of the main dynamics and drivers of emissions. Within this context, the interest in modelling and forecasting GHG emissions is without doubt. Carbon dioxide (CO 2) emissions, largely by-products of energy consumption, account for the largest share of GHG and, consequently, the analysis of GHG emissions has usually focused on CO 2 emissions; see, for instance, Friedlingstein et al. ( 2022 ), who describes the Global Carbon Project that produces world-wide projections of CO 2emissions in preparing the annual Global Carbon Budget, which is considered in the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPPC) reports.
